    FDA warning letters to peptide sellers in 2026: what happened.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 2 Nov 2026.

    Short answer

    From 1 January to 2 Nov 2026, the FDA sent 77 warning letters that our letters page tracks to peptide sellers, compounders and online clinics.1 55 went to online clinics and telehealth companies. The substances named most were semaglutide (69), tirzepatide (66) and retatrutide (10).1 The busiest months were February (31) and June (26). A letter asks the company to reply within 15 business days with the steps it took to fix the problems.2

    How many letters were there this year?

    Our letters page lists every FDA warning letter we find that names a peptide or goes to a seller in our database. This year it holds 77, out of 172 since 12 Jun 2023.1 The FDA posts its letters on fda.gov, where you can search them all.3

    By the month on the letter:

    FDA warning letters to peptide sellers by month, 2026
    MonthLetters
    January 20262
    February 202631
    March 20267
    April 20262
    May 20261
    June 202626
    July 20260
    August 20265
    September 20263
    October 20260
    November 20260

    Letters come in waves. The FDA often sends many on the same day to companies selling the same kind of product, so one busy month can hold most of a year.

    Which kinds of seller got them?

    We sort each letter by the seller we matched it to, or by the FDA's own subject when it says "Telehealth" or "Compounding Pharmacy":

    FDA warning letters by kind of seller, 2026
    Kind of sellerLetters
    Online clinics and telehealth companies55
    Research-use peptide shops11
    Other companies, such as internet pharmacies7
    Compounding pharmacies and prescription clinics4

    Online clinics sell a prescription after a visit; research-use shops sell vials labeled not for people. Our guide Online clinic vs research-use shop explains the difference.

    Which substances do the letters name?

    75 of this year's letters name at least one substance we track. Many name more than one, so the counts add up to more than the letters:1

    Substances named in FDA warning letters, 2026
    SubstanceLetters
    Semaglutide69
    Tirzepatide66
    Retatrutide10
    Bremelanotide5
    Tesamorelin5
    Elamipretide4

    Each count opens the letters that name it. Each name opens our page on that substance, with its FDA status.

    Semaglutide and tirzepatide are FDA approved as brand medicines, so these letters are about copies of them or about how they were sold. The FDA says it has warned companies selling these drugs labeled "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption".4

    What did the letters say was wrong?

    Every letter has a subject, the FDA's short label for the problem. The most common this year:

    • False & Misleading Claims/Misbranded: 55
    • Unapproved New Drugs/Misbranded: 7
    • Unapproved New Drugs Sold Over the Internet: 7
    • Compounding Pharmacy/Adulterated Drug Products: 4

    "Misbranded" means the label or the website says something the FDA believes is false or not allowed. "Unapproved new drug" means a product sold as a medicine without FDA approval.5 Our guide What an FDA warning letter means explains the words.

    What does a letter ask the company to do?

    The company is asked to reply in writing within 15 business days, with the steps it took to correct each problem, how it will stop them from happening again and copies of its papers. If it believes it did nothing wrong, it can send its reasons instead.2

    When the FDA has checked that the problems were really fixed, usually with a follow-up inspection, it may send a close-out letter. A promise to fix is not enough.5

    What does this mean for you?

    A letter is the FDA's view at the time, not a court ruling. A seller with a letter is still listed on our pages, with the letter linked, so you can read it and decide. Our weight loss page shows each clinic's newest letter, and every peptide page counts the letters that name it.

    This page counts again each time we pull our data. None of this is legal or medical advice.
